title: When Tea Goes Cold
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
My tea had gone cold twice before Iroh noticed.

The first time, he was finding a replacement kettle for a neighbor whose handle had broken. The second, he had promised a visiting merchant that he'd explain the difference between two jasmine blends, despite Mina being perfectly qualified to do it herself.

By the time he sat across from me, the shop was nearly empty.

"You're quiet," he said.

"I've been waiting to talk to you."

He blinked. "I'm here."

"I know. I've watched you pass this table six times."

That wasn't entirely fair. Every request had been real. The broken kettle could have burned somebody; the merchant had money to spend; the afternoon's accounts still needed signing. But I had planned to tell Iroh about an invitation to spend several days in Lanternweald, and each time I tried to start, something else became urgent.

Mina appeared with a stack of cups. "I can handle the front," she said.

"Are you sure?" Iroh asked.

"I'm sure because it's my shift. I would like you to stop asking me to prove it."

He looked chastened. I appreciated that he didn't turn her annoyance into a joke.

We moved to the back room, where rain tapped against the small window. Iroh poured another pot and let the leaves settle. I watched his hands. He had the movements of a man who could still measure time by ritual even when the rest of his day ran away from him.

"I don't want you to be my only priority," I said. "I want to know when we are actually making time for each other."

"I thought we were."

"We planned this afternoon. You said yes to three more things without telling me the plan had changed."

His face lost some of its gentleness. "People needed help."

"I know. And you chose to help them. I'm not angry that they matter."

"Then what are you angry about?"

"That I became the one person you assumed would understand indefinitely."

The answer sat between us. I wished I could take the sharpness out of it without losing the truth.

He looked toward the door. "I spent years trying to prove I could be of use after I'd done harm. It is easier to answer a stranger who asks for a kettle than someone who asks me to be present."

"Being present isn't a trick question."

"No," he said. "But I sometimes treat it as one."

I told him about the Lanternweald invitation. I wanted to visit Moonroot, see the noticeboard changes, and spend time with other people I loved. He had known from the beginning that I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory. We had agreed that invitations could be accepted or declined without punishment. Still, telling him I would be away felt awkward when we'd barely been together this week.

He asked which dates I was considering.

"From next Thursday until the following Monday. I haven't confirmed them. I wanted to talk to you first because we said we would have supper Friday."

"Ah."

"I'm not asking you to make the decision for me. I'm asking whether we can move our supper to Wednesday, or make a different plan."

He took a breath. "Wednesday would be lovely. I have no objection to the visit. I would have liked to hear about it before the shop closed."

"I was trying."

He winced.

"I see."

Mina came back before Iroh could rise for the kettle. She set a clean pot on the table and looked pointedly at the two of us.

"Tea is ready. Please do not create another reason for him to disappear into the storeroom."

Iroh looked offended. "I was merely going to check whether the water was hot enough."

"I have spent twelve years learning that," Mina replied.

I hid a laugh in my sleeve. She returned to the counter, leaving us a whole hour with no one asking for wisdom. The luxury of it made me uncertain what to do with my hands.

"Can I tell you what worried me about the invitation?" I asked.

"Of course."

"I thought you might hear that I was going away and decide it meant I was less serious about us."

He considered the words instead of rushing to reassure me.

"I thought that for a moment," he admitted. "Then I remembered what you told me about being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory. It is not an agreement that asks you to be present every hour."

"Knowing that doesn't make missing me easy."

"No. But I am allowed to miss you without making it a condition of your return."

I rested my hand on the table. He covered it briefly with his own.

"What would make our time here easier?" I asked.

"Perhaps I could close the door to the back room when I've promised you an hour, and ask Mina whether she wants that shift instead of assuming she can take it."

"And pay her for it."

"Yes."

We wrote the idea in the shop schedule. Mina read it before agreeing, because she had plans of her own. The next afternoon Iroh couldn't find his favorite tea tin and spent ten minutes accusing a spoon of conspiring against him. I laughed until my face hurt.

The shop wasn't becoming less important. Neither was I. We were simply learning to distinguish a true emergency from the habit of answering every call, even when someone we loved was already sitting in front of us.

We let the rain make the next few sounds. Then I pointed at the cold tea.

"Would you mind making me a new cup?"

He smiled, almost apologetically. "I thought you might ask."

"No philosophies about whether tea is ever truly cold."

"I would never."

He started to rise. I caught his sleeve.

"Not as an escape, Iroh. You can sit while the water heats."

He sat again.

We made an actual arrangement. On Wednesday, Mina would close according to her agreed schedule, and we would cook our own dinner after the shop finished. If a real emergency interrupted it, we would say so. If a request could wait, it would wait. He would stop offering my free time in the name of being generous. I would speak before my resentment became a silent test.

"That's a very long list," he said.

"You've negotiated peace between more difficult people."

"None of them knew how often I forgot their tea."

I laughed. He reached for my hand but waited until I offered it.

When he told Mina the new arrangement, she nodded approvingly and reminded him that she would not stay late to make it happen. He thanked her, and I believed he meant it.

The new tea was hot. I drank it slowly.

On Wednesday, he kept his word. The shop closed on time. He bought mushrooms and rice on the way home and cooked without narrating a lesson about patience. We argued cheerfully over whether the mushrooms needed more salt. At the sink, I leaned against his shoulder and listened to him hum.

"Was this worth a whole afternoon of difficult conversation?" he asked.

"Absolutely."

"Even though the tea went cold?"

"Especially because of that."

He set the dishcloth aside. I asked whether I could kiss him. He said yes, and his answer had a pleased, almost bashful quality that made my chest ache.

We left the kitchen tidy enough for the morning, closed the bedroom door and kept the rest of the evening private.

The next time a merchant interrupted our planned hour, Iroh asked Mina whether she had the sale handled. She did. He came back to our table.

The tea stayed warm because we were there to drink it.
